Here's my take on this entire debacle.

San Bernardino county is negligent and technically incompetent, at least as much as the federal government is with regards to this issue. My reasoning? Mobile Device Management.

MDM is EXTREMELY COMMON in the private IT world, and virtually unknown in government and federal employment. Most companies that issue phones to employees have it now. What is it? It's a software/server package that mobile devices (tablets, phones, laptops, etc) are "enrolled" into that:

  1. grants the user access to things like secure company email, company apps, secure documents and secure browsing of intranet, etc
  2. It grants the employer control over the device from a management standpoint. We can access the GPS data, control app installs, data backup settings, UNLOCK PHONES locked with pins, decrypt devices, etc.
  3. we can also enforce security standards... like not letting Joe User from the TopSecretHR to have his company issued iPhone pin be "1111" or making sure Secretary of State IWantMyOwnMailServer can't access email systems other than the proscribed official server.

If one this was one of my users phones the feds had, they wouldn't even need to talk to apple, after all it's MY phone, not the users. I simply log into my console and reset the PIN to 1234 and let the feds have at it. It's not a privacy concern because it's not the users phone, and this was a condition as part of the issuance of the device (like your company laptop or PC). If you "remove" the software from your phone (because you want to be sneaky for 6 weeks before your terrorist attack) then

  1. the second you disable the function, I get notified. I contact you asking WTF and your boss gets copied on the message
  2. 2 hours after you disabled the functions, your phone locks itself out and you have to contact me to get it working again
  3. 24hrs with no contact and it's an actionable offense. I.E. disciplinary action against you

Additionally, the FBI isn't even trying. Comey came out today and issued a statement that "We simply want the chance, with a search warrant, to try to guess the terrorist's passcode without the phone essentially self-destructing" Well guess what dumbass? You can do that now. Powering off the device resets the incorrect PIN counter. It's a 4 digit pin, so we're not even talking insane numbers here. 10,000 possible combinations. If you have some expendable FBI intern punch in 12 passwords an hour (3, reboot, 3 reboot, 3 reboot, 3 reboot) then you'd have it "cracked" in less than 100 days. It's not like this is some kind of Jack Bauer 24 situation. The guy is dead and by their own admission the just want to do "a little more due diligence" in the investigation.

In short, the government doesn't NEED apple to compromise the security of every goddamn phone in existence. It needs drag itself into the modern age and enforce common sense device management both federally AND locally. If anything the feds should be pushing Apple/Google to make MDM solutions even MORE capable (like Blackberry used to). This would allow private phone owners all the encryption and privacy they (and I) want, allowing companies to ebrace mobile devices more readily and enforcing some actual common sense security on government departments, who desperately need it.
